h1: What SEO pays, by role and by country
metaTitle: How Much Does SEO Pay? Roles and Countries
metaDescription: How much does SEO pay across roles and markets? Compare Indian in-house, Indian agency, freelance and remote-for-overseas pay, with real INR ranges.
answer: The same SEO skill pays four very different numbers. An Indian agency role runs roughly ₹3–₹12 lakh a year, in-house at a product company ₹6–₹22 lakh, freelance ₹25,000–₹2,00,000 a month depending on how many retainers you hold, and remote work for US or UK clients commonly three to five times the agency figure.
takeaways: Your **route to market** moves your pay more than your years of experience do. Same person, four employers, four wildly different numbers.
Agencies pay least and teach fastest. Product companies pay most for the same title. That trade is real and worth making deliberately.
Remote-for-overseas is the biggest single jump available to an Indian SEO — and it's a **sales and communication** test as much as a skills test.
Freelance income isn't a salary with more upside. It's revenue minus tools, tax, unbilled hours and the months you're between clients.

body: Take one competent SEO with four or five years' experience. Depending only on who pays them, their annual income can vary by a factor of six. Nothing about their skill changes across these rows — only who the buyer is and what currency the buyer earns in.
These are market ranges we see in hiring, offers and client conversations. Not survey data. Nobody publishes a reliable SEO pay census in India, and any page quoting one to the rupee made it up.

callout.title: Read the variance column
callout.body: The top two rows are salaries: they arrive on the same date every month whether or not you had a good quarter. The bottom two are revenue. People compare row four to row one and conclude the agency job is foolish, which ignores that row four has no notice period, no health cover and no floor.

sections.h2: Indian agency versus in-house: same title, different number
body: For an identical title and identical years, an Indian product company or funded startup typically pays 30–60% more than a domestic services agency. That's arithmetic, not unfairness. An agency's salary budget is a slice of a retainer that must also cover four disciplines, tools, management and margin.

What the agency gives back is range. Two years agency-side means fifteen sites, three migrations, four verticals and every kind of broken analytics setup. Two years in-house means knowing one site extremely well. Both are valuable, at different points.

The pattern that pays best over a decade is boring: two to four years agency-side to collect reps, then move in-house or to a product company at the specialist or manager band and take the raise. In the other order you tend to end up knowing one site deeply and struggling to diagnose an unfamiliar one.
bullets: **Export-facing Indian agencies pay above domestic ones** for identical experience, often 20–40% more, because their revenue is in dollars and pounds and their competition for that person is global.
**Marketplaces, D2C brands and fintechs** pay at the top of the in-house range, because organic traffic maps onto revenue in a way everyone in the building can see.
**Traditional enterprises pay mid-band** but often have the most interesting technical problems — worth something if you're building toward the technical route.

sections.h2: Freelance: what the per-project maths actually looks like
body: The number that matters isn't your rate. It's your rate multiplied by utilisation — the share of working hours you actually bill. Most freelancers land between 50% and 65% once you count sales calls, proposals, invoicing, chasing payments and the gaps between contracts. A ₹1,00,000/month retainer looks like a good salary until you notice you held three of them for seven months and one for five.

callout.title: The three deductions people forget
callout.body: Tools are ₹15,000–₹25,000 a month and you can't work without a crawler and a backlink index. GST registration applies once you cross the threshold and changes what you can quote. And there's no paid leave — every holiday is unbilled. Take your annual revenue, cut 25–30%, and compare that against an offer.

sections.h2: Remote for overseas clients: the three-to-five-times route
body: This is the largest single pay jump available to an Indian SEO, and it exists for one unglamorous reason: the client prices against what the work costs in their market, not yours. A retainer in the low thousands of dollars a month is cheap to a US or UK company and a very large number in rupees.

That's currency arbitrage, and it's real. It's also narrower than the LinkedIn version suggests, because overseas buyers aren't hiring hands — they can already buy hands cheaply from a hundred agencies. They're buying judgment and someone they can rely on without supervision.

Rates move with the dollar and the pound, so treat any INR figure as a live range rather than a quote. What's stable is the ratio: work sold into a high-wage market pays a multiple of the same work sold domestically.
bullets: **What they buy:** diagnosis, strategy, technical depth, and writing that survives being forwarded to their CEO.
**What they won't pay a premium for:** publishing, meta tags, outreach volume, reporting. Commodity tasks with a global floor price.
**The hidden requirement:** overlap hours. IST to US Eastern means late evenings; IST to UK means afternoons. Nobody mentions it in the pitch and everyone feels it by month three.
**The real risk:** client concentration. Two clients paying well feels like a great year until one restructures. Three is the minimum that lets you sleep.

**Getting in:** most people arrive via an export-facing Indian agency first, because it teaches the communication standard on someone else's account. [Indian agencies serving global clients](/journal/indian-agencies-serving-global-clients) covers how that market works.

callout.title: Freelance is a sales job with SEO attached
callout.body: This is the misjudgement that ends most freelance attempts inside eighteen months. The SEO part is the part you already know. Whether you earn ₹4 lakh or ₹40 lakh depends on whether you can find and close clients repeatedly. If you dislike selling, the remote-employee route pays similarly and asks far less of that muscle.

body: City still moves the number more than most people expect. Remote hiring narrowed the gap; it didn't close it, because employers benchmark against local cost of living and against who else is bidding for the person. Roughly, against a national mid-band:
bullets: **Bengaluru and Gurugram / Delhi NCR** sit at the top of every band — the largest concentration of product companies and export-facing agencies bidding for the same shortlist.
**Mumbai** is close behind, weighted toward media, D2C and BFSI. High pay, and the highest cost of living to spend it in.
**Pune, Hyderabad and Chennai** typically run 10–20% below Bengaluru for the same role, with enough product-company presence to keep senior bands competitive.
**Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Indore, Kochi and Coimbatore** run 20–35% below the metros. Real services hubs with real work, but far fewer employers competing for you — which is what actually sets pay.
**Fully remote for an Indian employer** lands between the two: better than a tier-2 local job, below a metro in-office offer, and closing slowly.

body: Three patterns hold across every route on this page, and none are about knowing more SEO facts.

Pay tracks **accountability**, not output — the person who decides what to kill earns multiples of the person who executes it well. Pay tracks **who your work is sold to**: the same audit is worth ₹25,000 to a small Indian business and ten times that to a US SaaS company, because it protects a much larger revenue number. And pay tracks **scarcity of the combination** — SEO alone is common, SEO plus engineering or data or a regulated vertical is not, which is the argument laid out in full on [is SEO a high paying skill](/answers/is-seo-a-high-paying-skill).
For the detailed Indian ladder — intern to head of SEO, with monthly figures and city multipliers — [SEO salaries in India](/answers/what-is-the-salary-of-seo-in-india) has the full table.

faqs.a: It pays badly at entry level and well past the specialist band. In India the first two years typically run ₹2,40,000–₹4,50,000 a year, which is poor. A technical specialist or manager at ₹12–₹25 lakh is paid comparably to other senior marketing roles, and remote work for overseas clients goes well past that.

faqs.q: Which pays more, SEO or paid ads?
faqs.a: At junior level they're close. At senior level, performance marketers managing large budgets often edge ahead in-house because the number they control is visible daily, while senior technical SEO and organic leads at product companies match or beat them. The bigger difference is temperament: fast feedback and daily pressure versus slow feedback and quarterly pressure.

faqs.q: How much does a freelance SEO earn in India?
faqs.a: Anywhere from ₹3,00,000 to ₹24,00,000 a year, and the range is wide because it's revenue, not salary. Typical retainers run ₹15,000–₹75,000 per client per month with three to five concurrent clients as a realistic solo ceiling. Subtract 25–30% for tools, tax, unbilled time and gaps between contracts.

faqs.q: Can an Indian SEO earn in dollars?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's the biggest single pay jump in the field — commonly three to five times a domestic agency salary, because the client prices against their own market. What they're buying is judgment and unsupervised reliability, not production. It also costs you overlap hours and adds client-concentration risk.

faqs.q: How much does an SEO manager earn?
faqs.a: In India, roughly ₹12,00,000–₹25,00,000 a year, with Bengaluru, Gurugram and Mumbai at the top of that band and tier-2 cities 20–35% below. The jump to that band happens when you own the plan and the number in front of a founder, not when you hit five years' experience.

faqs.q: Is SEO pay going up or down?
faqs.a: Both, in different places. The entry band is under pressure because the tasks that define it are the most automatable ones. The technical, analytical and strategic bands are holding or rising, partly because the tier below them is thinning and fewer people are being trained into the senior roles.
